claim: HLA class I presentation of pathogen-derived peptide ligands is essential for CD8+ T-cell recognition of Toxoplasma gondii infected cells.
source: HLA class I presentation of pathogen-derived peptide ligands is essential for CD8+ T-cell recognition of Toxoplasma gondii infected cells.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a foundational premise of the study.

claim: Currently, little data exist pertaining to peptides that are presented after T. gondii infection.
source: Currently, little data exist pertaining to peptides that are presented after T. gondii infection.
evidence: This statement reflects the state of knowledge in the field at the time of the study.

claim: 195 T. gondii encoded ligands were identified originating from both secreted and cytoplasmic proteins.
source: We identify 195 T. gondii encoded ligands originating from both secreted and cytoplasmic proteins.
evidence: This is a primary finding reported in the abstract and supported by mass spectrometry data.

claim: T. gondii ligands are significantly longer than uninfected host ligands.
source: Surprisingly, T. gondii ligands are significantly longer than uninfected host ligands, and these longer pathogen-derived peptides maintain a canonical N-terminal binding core yet exhibit a C-terminal extension of 1–30 amino acids.
evidence: This is supported by length distribution analysis and statistical comparison (t-test, p<0.001) shown in Figure 5.

claim: T. gondii ligands maintain a canonical N-terminal binding core yet exhibit a C-terminal extension of 1–30 amino acids.
source: Surprisingly, T. gondii ligands are significantly longer than uninfected host ligands, and these longer pathogen-derived peptides maintain a canonical N-terminal binding core yet exhibit a C-terminal extension of 1–30 amino acids.
evidence: This is supported by computational prediction analysis and binding assays.

claim: Binding of extended peptides opens the HLA class I F' pocket, allowing the C-terminal extension to protrude through one end of the binding groove.
source: Structural analysis demonstrates that binding of extended peptides opens the HLA class I F' pocket, allowing the C-terminal extension to protrude through one end of the binding groove.
evidence: This is demonstrated by crystallographic structures of HLA-A*02:01 complexed with extended peptides (PDB IDs 5D9S and 5DDH).

claim: CD8 T-cells mediate immunity to Toxoplasma gondii infection through recognition of peptide antigens presented by the MHC class I molecules of infected cells.
source: CD8 T-cells mediate immunity to Toxoplasma gondii infection (Khan et al., 1988; Suzuki and Remington, 1988) through recognition of peptide antigens presented by the MHC class I (MHC I) molecules of infected cells (Brown and McLeod, 1990; Deckert-Schlüter et al., 1994).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: The majority of peptide ligands identified to date are derived from parasite surface proteins, proteins localized to dense granules, or the rhoptry proteins.
source: The majority of peptide ligands identified to date are derived from parasite surface proteins, proteins localized to dense granules, or the rhoptry proteins which are specialized secretory granules whose contents are released either into the host cell cytoplasm or the parasitophorous vacuole (Blanchard et al., 2008; Cardona et al., 2015; Cong et al., 2011).
evidence: This is based on prior literature as indicated by citations.

claim: Secreted proteins are thought to be optimal candidates for MHC I presentation because they have the best access to conventional antigen processing and presentation machinery in the host cell.
source: These secreted proteins are thought to be optimal candidates for MHC I presentation because they have the best access to conventional antigen processing and presentation machinery in the host cell.
evidence: This represents a hypothesis or prevailing view in the field.

claim: MHC I molecules present a considerable number of peptides >11 amino acids that elicit T-cell responses.
source: While a majority of peptides are 8–11 amino acids in length, MHC I molecules present a considerable number of peptides >11 amino acids (Hassan et al., 2015; Schittenhelm et al., 2014) that elicit T-cell responses (Hassan et al., 2015; Burrows et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Long MHC I ligands interact with the MHC I molecule with the peptide anchored by their second (P2) and C-terminal (PΩ) residues, with the middle portion bulging out of the groove.
source: Structural characterizations suggest that these long ligands interact with the MHC I molecule much like canonical peptides: The MHC I alpha chain forms a 10 x 25 angstrom groove in which peptide ligands are anchored by their second (P2) and C-terminal (PΩ) residues. In this mode of binding, the middle portion of any oversized peptides can bulge out of the MHC I groove and interact with the receptors of T lymphocytes (Tynan et al., 2005).
evidence: This is based on prior structural characterizations cited in the text.

claim: A structural example exists of a 10mer interacting with HLA-A2 via P2 and P9 with an amino acid extension at P10.
source: Crystallographic studies have confirmed this bulging model, although there exists a structural example of a 10mer interacting with MHC I molecule HLA-A2 via P2 and P9 with an amino acid extension at P10 (Collins et al., 1994).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a crystallographic study.

claim: Over the course of a 1-week infection, the number of infected THP-1 cells increased from 12.1% day 1 post infection to 71.5% on day 7 post infection.
source: Over the course of a 1-week infection, the number of infected cells increased from 12.1% day 1 post infection to 71.5% on day 7 post infection (Figure 1).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1.

claim: A steady increase in the number of free parasites in the culture media from day 1 to 7 was indicative of a productive infection.
source: A steady increase in the number of free parasites in the culture media from day 1 to 7 was indicative of a productive infection.
evidence: This is based on parasite count data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: 12 mg HLA-A*02:01 was produced from infected cells.
source: The production of 12 mg HLA-A*02:01 from infected cells was sufficient for a comprehensive analysis of T. gondii peptide ligands.
evidence: This is a reported measurement from the purification process.

claim: A total of 284 peptide sequences precisely matched the reported sequence of T. gondii.
source: A total of 284 peptide sequences precisely matched the reported sequence of T. gondii.
evidence: This is a result from mass spectrometry analysis.

claim: 89 of the T. gondii-matching peptides were either an exact match or contained an isobaric Ile/Leu ambiguity match to sequences of the H. sapiens host species.
source: Strikingly, 89 of these peptides were either an exact match or contained an isobaric Ile/Leu ambiguity match to sequences of the H. sapiens host species (Supplementary file 1), leaving 195 ligands definitively derived from T. gondii (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is based on sequence comparison analysis.

claim: Of the confirmed T. gondii derived ligands, 159 show little (<50%) similarity to H. sapiens while 36 peptides have >50% similarity.
source: Of these confirmed T. gondii derived ligands, most (159) show little (<50%) similarity to H. sapiens while 36 peptides have >50% similarity.
evidence: This is based on BLAST analysis of sequences.

claim: 31% of the T. gondii derived ligands are identical to H. sapiens sequences, 13% show host similarity, and 56% have no similarity to host proteins.
source: In summary, 31% of the T. gondii derived ligands are identical to H. sapiens sequences, 13% show host similarity, and 56% of the T. gondii ligands have no similarity to host proteins (Figure 2).
evidence: This is based on sequence similarity analysis shown in Figure 2.

claim: The 195 T. gondii ligands identified originate from 95 different proteins of which 87 are non-GRA proteins.
source: In our dataset, the 195 T. gondii ligands identified originate from 95 different proteins of which 87 are non-GRA proteins, demonstrating that a considerable number of proteins are accessible to MHC I presentation.
evidence: This is based on analysis of the source proteins of identified ligands.

claim: For 55.8% of the T. gondii source proteins a single peptide was presented.
source: For 55.8% of the T. gondii source proteins a single peptide was presented (Figure 3A), while elongation factor 1 alpha provided 12 peptide ligands.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Elongation factor 1 alpha provided 12 peptide ligands.
source: For 55.8% of the T. gondii source proteins a single peptide was presented (Figure 3A), while elongation factor 1 alpha provided 12 peptide ligands.
evidence: This is based on analysis of source proteins.

claim: Peptide ligand enrichment from particular proteins was not due to protein length as median protein lengths were not statistically different regardless of the number of ligands embedded within a protein.
source: Peptide ligand enrichment from particular proteins was not due to protein length as median protein lengths were not statistically different (Kruskal-Wallis test, p = 0.247) regardless of the number of ligands embedded within a protein (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis (Kruskal-Wallis test) shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: 30 GRA ligands (15%) were observed with GRA12 providing the most peptide ligands.
source: Dense granule proteins have been reported as a source of peptides (Blanchard et al., 2008; Cardona et al., 2015; Cong et al., 2010; 2011; 2012; El Bissati et al., 2014), and here 30 GRA ligands (15%) were observed with GRA12 providing the most (Hassan et al., 2015) peptide ligands (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is based on analysis of source proteins shown in Figure 3C.

claim: There was a significant enrichment in proteins localized to the apical part of the T. gondii cell (GO:0045177, p = 1.50 x 10-8).
source: There was a significant enrichment in proteins localized to the apical part of the T. gondii cell (GO:0045177, p = 1.50 x 10-8) and to the parasitophorous vacuole (GO:0020003, p = 2.79 x 10-6).
evidence: This is based on Gene Ontology enrichment analysis.

claim: There was a significant enrichment in proteins localized to the parasitophorous vacuole (GO:0020003, p = 2.79 x 10-6).
source: There was a significant enrichment in proteins localized to the apical part of the T. gondii cell (GO:0045177, p = 1.50 x 10-8) and to the parasitophorous vacuole (GO:0020003, p = 2.79 x 10-6).
evidence: This is based on Gene Ontology enrichment analysis.

claim: There was a significant enrichment in proteins originating from the parasite cytoplasm (GO:0005737, p = 9.31 x 10-4) with 21 of 95 proteins annotated as cytoplasmic.
source: Unexpectedly, there was a significant enrichment in proteins originating from the parasite cytoplasm (GO:0005737, p = 9.31 x 10-4) with 21 of 95 proteins annotated as cytoplasmic.
evidence: This is based on Gene Ontology enrichment analysis.

claim: When T. gondii ligands were compared to the baseline uninfected ligand distribution there was a significant reduction in N-terminal peptides (bins 0–0.2, p = 2.36 x 10-4 and 0.2–0.4, p = 2.23 x 10-4).
source: When the T. gondii ligands were compared to the baseline uninfected ligand distribution there was a significant reduction in N-terminal peptides (bins 0–0.2, p = 2.36 x 10-4 and 0.2–0.4, p = 2.23 x 10-4, comparison of proportions) along with significant enrichment in ligands from the C-terminal end of the protein (bins 0.6–0.8, p = 1.46 x 10-2 and 0.8–1.0, p = 5.26 x 10-7).
evidence: This is based on statistical comparison of normalized ligand positions shown in Figure 4.

claim: There was significant enrichment in T. gondii ligands from the C-terminal end of the protein (bins 0.6–0.8, p = 1.46 x 10-2 and 0.8–1.0, p = 5.26 x 10-7).
source: When the T. gondii ligands were compared to the baseline uninfected ligand distribution there was a significant reduction in N-terminal peptides (bins 0–0.2, p = 2.36 x 10-4 and 0.2–0.4, p = 2.23 x 10-4, comparison of proportions) along with significant enrichment in ligands from the C-terminal end of the protein (bins 0.6–0.8, p = 1.46 x 10-2 and 0.8–1.0, p = 5.26 x 10-7).
evidence: This is based on statistical comparison of normalized ligand positions shown in Figure 4.

claim: T. gondii ligands are significantly enriched from the C-terminal end of their source proteins.
source: In summary, T. gondii ligands are significantly enriched from the C-terminal end of their source proteins and host-derived peptide ligands shift towards the C-termini of their respective source proteins following infection.
evidence: This is based on normalized ligand position analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: Host-derived peptide ligands shift towards the C-termini of their respective source proteins following infection.
source: In summary, T. gondii ligands are significantly enriched from the C-terminal end of their source proteins and host-derived peptide ligands shift towards the C-termini of their respective source proteins following infection.
evidence: This is based on comparison of host ligands from infected vs uninfected cells shown in Figure 4.

claim: T. gondii ligands were significantly longer (t-test, p<0.001) with an average length of 14.6 amino acids compared with 11.4 amino acids in the host ligands from the infected cells.
source: When compared with the host-derived ligands, the T. gondii ligands were significantly longer (t-test, p<0.001) with an average length of 14.6 amino acids compared with 11.4 amino acids in the host ligands from the infected cells and with 9.8 for uninfected host ligands.
evidence: This is based on statistical comparison of peptide lengths shown in Figure 5.

claim: Host ligands from infected cells had an average length of 11.4 amino acids compared with 9.8 for uninfected host ligands, and this increase was statistically significant (t-test, p<0.001).
source: When compared with the host-derived ligands, the T. gondii ligands were significantly longer (t-test, p<0.001) with an average length of 14.6 amino acids compared with 11.4 amino acids in the host ligands from the infected cells and with 9.8 for uninfected host ligands. This increase in host ligand length following infection was statistically significant (t-test, p<0.001).
evidence: This is based on statistical comparison of peptide lengths shown in Figure 5.

claim: NetMHCpan 2.8 predicted that 117 of 195 ligands (60%) bind at a percentile rank score <=10%, leaving 78 predicted non-binders.
source: NetMHCpan 2.8 predicted that 117 of 195 ligands (60%) bind at a percentile rank score <=10%, leaving 78 predicted non-binders (Figure 6).
evidence: This is based on computational binding predictions shown in Figure 6.

claim: A considerable number (52/78) of the predicted non-binders contained nested core sequences of 8–11 amino acids that were predicted to bind with high affinity (percentile rank score <=2%).
source: A subsequent search revealed nested core sequences of 8–11 amino acids within the longer peptides that were not predicted to bind, and these cores were predicted to bind to HLA-A*02:01. Strikingly, a considerable number (52/78) of the predicted non-binders contained nested core sequences of 8–11 amino acids that were predicted to bind with high affinity (percentile rank score <=2%).
evidence: This is based on computational analysis of nested binding cores.

claim: The proportion of predicted non-binders containing nested binding cores (52/78) was significantly more (p = 1.2 x 10-10) than if the sequences were randomly scrambled (13/78).
source: This was significantly more (p = 1.2 x 10-10, comparison of proportions) than if the sequences were randomly scrambled (13/78).
evidence: This is based on statistical comparison with scrambled sequences.

claim: Most (36/52) binding cores within T. gondii ligands were at the very N-terminus with the peptide extending from the core's C-terminus.
source: Within the T. gondii ligands, most (36/52) binding cores were at the very N-terminus with the peptide extending from the core's C-terminus (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is based on analysis of binding core positions.

claim: N-terminal binding cores in T. gondii ligands occurred significantly more (p = 3.1 x 10-5) than in randomly scrambled versions of the peptides (1/13).
source: This occurred significantly more than randomly scrambled versions of the peptides (1/13) (p = 3.1 x 10-5, comparison of proportions).
evidence: This is based on statistical comparison with scrambled sequences.

claim: Among the N-terminal binders, the average C-terminal extension was 8.7 amino acids and the extension varied considerably from 1 to 30 amino acids.
source: Among the N-terminal binders, the average C-terminal extension was 8.7 amino acids and the extension varied considerably from 1 to 30 amino acids (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is based on analysis of extension lengths.

claim: Among ligands from uninfected cells, 2.3% had a C-terminal extension - the baseline of extended peptides in uninfected THP-1 cells.
source: Among ligands from uninfected cells, 2.3% had a C-terminal extension - the baseline of extended peptides in uninfected THP-1 cells.
evidence: This is based on analysis of ligands from uninfected cells shown in Figure 6.

claim: After T. gondii infection, the percentage of host ligands with a C-terminal extension significantly increased to 7.2% (p<0.0001).
source: After T. gondii infection, the percentage of host ligands with a C-terminal extension significantly increased to 7.2% (p<0.0001, comparison of proportions) (Figure 6), a percentage that is less than half the T. gondii derived ligands with extensions (18.5%).
evidence: This is based on statistical comparison shown in Figure 6.

claim: 18.5% of T. gondii derived ligands had C-terminal extensions.
source: After T. gondii infection, the percentage of host ligands with a C-terminal extension significantly increased to 7.2% (p<0.0001, comparison of proportions) (Figure 6), a percentage that is less than half the T. gondii derived ligands with extensions (18.5%).
evidence: This is based on analysis of T. gondii ligands shown in Figure 6.

claim: Of twelve tested ligands, eight binding cores bound with high affinity (<500 nM), three with moderate affinity (<1000 nM), and one had no affinity.
source: Of these 12 peptides, eight binding cores bound with high affinity (<500 nM), three with moderate affinity (<1000 nM), and one had no affinity – the N-terminal cores overwhelmingly bound to HLA-A*02:01.
evidence: This is based on competitive binding assay data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Two of the twelve full-length ligands (YLSPIASPLLDGKSLR-RPL7A15-30 and FVLELEPEWTVK-UFP16-27) bound with high affinity even though predictions ranked them as non-binders.
source: Two of the twelve full-length ligands (YLSPIASPLLDGKSLR-RPL7A15-30) and FVLELEPEWTVK-UFP16-27) also bound with high affinity (Figure 7A) even though predictions ranked them as non-binders as their C-termini were incompatible with the HLA-A*02:01 binding motif.
evidence: This is based on competitive binding assay data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: For FVLELEPEWTVK, the affinity of all 'mutant' peptides was significantly worse (t-test, p<0.05) than either the binding core or the native full-length peptide.
source: For FVLELEPEWTVK, the affinity of all 'mutant' peptides was significantly worse (t-test, p<0.05) than either the binding core or the native full-length peptide (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is based on binding assay data with mutant peptides shown in Figure 7B.

claim: With YLSPIASPLLDGKSLR, all but one (L10E) of the mutants had a lower binding affinity in comparison to the wild type sequence (t-test, p<0.05).
source: With YLSPIASPLLDGKSLR, all but one (L10E) of the mutants had a lower binding affinity in comparison to the wild type sequence (t-test, p<0.05) (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is based on binding assay data with mutant peptides shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The melting temperature (Tm) for the two extended ligands exceeded 62°C (YLSPIASPLLDGKSLR, Tm = 66° C, FVLELEPEWTVK Tm = 63°C).
source: The melting temperature (Tm) for the two extended ligands exceeded 62°C (YLSPIASPLLDGKSLR, Tm = 66° C, FVLELEPEWTVK Tm = 63°C), temperatures that are consistent with ligands of conventional length (Hassan et al., 2015).
evidence: This is based on thermal denaturation assay data shown in Figure 8.

claim: The thermostability of the binding cores was at least 10°C higher (YLSPIASPLLDGKSLR, ΔTm = 10°C, FVLELEPEWTVK ΔTm = 12°C) than their extended counterparts.
source: It was somewhat surprising that these extended ligands had Tm representative of canonical ligands, and more remarkable was that the thermostability of the binding cores was at least 10°C higher (YLSPIASPLLDGKSLR, ΔTm = 10°C, FVLELEPEWTVK ΔTm = 12°C) than their extended counterparts (Figure 8).
evidence: This is based on thermal denaturation assay data shown in Figure 8.

claim: The structures of HLA-A*02:01 in complex with FVLELEPEWTVK and FVLELEPEWTV were solved at a resolution of 1.5 Å and 1.87Å, respectively.
source: To determine how C-terminal extensions protrude from the F' pocket of MHC I, we bound the extended ligand FVLELEPEWTVK (UFP16-27) and its binding core FVLELEPEWTV (UFP16-26) to HLA-A*02:01, crystallized these two complexes, and solved their structures at a resolution of 1.5 Å and 1.87Å, respectively (Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is based on X-ray crystallography data (PDB IDs 5D9S and 5DDH).

claim: Both peptides FVLELEPEWTVK and FVLELEPEWTV bound in a zig-zag fashion in order to accommodate the core 11 amino acids in the antigen-binding groove.
source: Both peptides bound in a zig-zag fashion in order to accommodate the core 11 amino acids in the antigen-binding groove (Figure 9A).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis shown in Figure 9A.

claim: The 11 amino acid core of extended ligand FVLELEPEWTVK interacts with HLA-A*02:01 in an almost identical manner to the shorter peptide, however, both the main chain and side chain of C-terminal Lys12 protrudes out the end of the binding pocket.
source: The 11 amino acid core of extended ligand FVLELEPEWTVK interacts with HLA-A*02:01 in an almost identical manner to the shorter peptide, however, both the main chain and side chain of C-terminal Lys12 protrudes out the end of the binding pocket (Figure 9B).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis shown in Figure 9B.

claim: For HLA-A*02:01 in complex with FVLELEPEWTVK, the side chain of Tyr84 swung up and out by almost 90 degrees, opening the binding groove so that a peptide might protrude from the groove at its C-termini.
source: However, for HLA-A*02:01 in complex with FVLELEPEWTVK, the side chain of Tyr84 swung up and out by almost 90 degrees (Figure 9A,F), opening the binding groove so that a peptide might protrude from the groove at its C-termini.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis shown in Figure 9F.

claim: Thr80 adopted a different rotamer when HLA-A*02:01 was in complex with FVLELEPEWTVK, further opening the MHC I pocket toward the end of the α1-helix.
source: At the same time, Thr80 adopted a different rotamer, further opening the MHC I pocket toward the end of the α1-helix.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis shown in Figure 9F.

claim: There was a subtle but noticeable increase in the main chain distance between the α1 and α2-helices at the F' pocket when HLA-A*02:01 was in complex with FVLELEPEWTVK.
source: Lastly, there was a subtle but noticeable increase in the main chain distance between the α 1 and α2-helices at the F' pocket (Figure 9G).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis shown in Figure 9G.

claim: Dense granule proteins are the best-characterized source of peptides for presentation by MHC I.
source: Indeed, the secreted dense granule proteins are the best-characterized source of peptides for presentation by MHC I, and our study confirms these proteins provide a number of MHC I ligands (Blanchard et al., 2008; Cardona et al., 2015; Cong et al., 2011).
evidence: This is based on prior literature and confirmed by the current study's data.

claim: Many of the ligands observed originate from non-secreted proteins, including parasite cytoplasmic proteins.
source: However, many of the ligands we observe originate from non-secreted proteins, including parasite cytoplasmic proteins.
evidence: This is based on analysis of source proteins and their cellular localization.

claim: Enrichment in cytoplasmic proteins is unexpected given that most T. gondii cytoplasmic proteins are not secreted and their cellular location should sequester them from the MHC I peptide processing machinery.
source: Enrichment in these proteins is unexpected given that most T. gondii cytoplasmic proteins are not secreted and their cellular location should sequester them from the MHC I peptide processing machinery.
evidence: This represents an inference based on known biology of T. gondii and MHC I processing.

claim: A little less than half (10/22) of the hypothetical proteins contain a predicted secretion signal sequence.
source: Additionally, a little less than half (10/22) of the hypothetical proteins contain a predicted secretion signal sequence.
evidence: This is based on computational prediction of signal sequences.

claim: A previous study indicated that ligands derived from the C-termini of T. gondii source proteins are immunodominant.
source: A previous study of MHC I and T. gondii indicated that ligands derived from the C-termini of T. gondii source proteins are immunodominant (Feliu et al., 2013), and it was suggested that a proteolytic insufficiency within infected murine cells meant that only peptides derived from the C-termini of T. gondii source proteins would provide ligands of optimal length (Feliu et al., 2013).
evidence: This is based on a citation to prior research.

claim: It was suggested that a proteolytic insufficiency within infected murine cells meant that only peptides derived from the C-termini of T. gondii source proteins would provide ligands of optimal length.
source: A previous study of MHC I and T. gondii indicated that ligands derived from the C-termini of T. gondii source proteins are immunodominant (Feliu et al., 2013), and it was suggested that a proteolytic insufficiency within infected murine cells meant that only peptides derived from the C-termini of T. gondii source proteins would provide ligands of optimal length (Feliu et al., 2013).
evidence: This is based on a citation to prior research.

claim: C-terminally extended peptides are presented by membrane-bound HLA-A*02:01.
source: A review of published ligand elution data confirms that C-terminally extended peptides are presented by membrane-bound HLA-A*02:01(Hassan et al., 2015; Chen et al., 1994; Scull et al., 2012), yet the considerable number of extended ligands observed in this in vitro model of T. gondii antigen processing and presentation merits future confirmation in vivo.
evidence: This is based on citations to prior published data.

claim: Structural support for the binding of extended peptide ligands in HLA-A*02:01 can be found in a calreticulin peptide example where the nonamer binding core is extended by a single C-terminal amino acid that fits within the MHC I groove.
source: That notwithstanding, structural support for the binding of extended peptide ligands in HLA-A*02:01 can also be found (Collins et al., 1994). In this example the nonamer binding core of a calreticulin peptide is extended by a single C-terminal amino acid that fits within the MHC I groove, yet this model was not consistent with T. gondii ligands that had as many as 30 C-terminally appended amino acids.
evidence: This is based on a citation to prior structural work.

claim: Tyr84 emerged as a 'swinging gate' whereby a longer T. gondii peptide extended straight out the end of the HLA molecule at its C-terminus when Tyr84 assumed an alternate up and out position.
source: As such, Tyr84 emerged as a "swinging gate" whereby a longer T. gondii peptide extended straight out the end of the HLA molecule at its C-terminus when Tyr84 assumed an alternate up and out position – the open gate.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis of the crystal structures.

claim: This structural configuration is distinct from c-terminal extensions previously reported with C-terminal extension of covalently linked peptides and predicted configurations where the peptide travels up and over Tyr84.
source: This structural configuration is distinct from c-terminal extensions previously reported with C-terminal extension of covalently linked peptides (Mitaksov et al., 2007) and predicted configurations (Hörig et al., 1999) where the peptide travels up and over Tyr84.
evidence: This is based on comparison with prior structural and computational studies.

claim: Tyr84 modestly rotated to facilitate the reported binding of calretulin to HLA-A*02:01.
source: Note that Tyr84 modestly rotated to facilitate the reported binding of calretulin to HLA-A*02:01 (Collins et al., 1994), and the gate-open displacement of Tyr84 observed here confirms that the MHC I binding pocket is less rigid than previously realized.
evidence: This is based on a citation to prior structural work.

claim: The gate-open displacement of Tyr84 observed here confirms that the MHC I binding pocket is less rigid than previously realized.
source: Note that Tyr84 modestly rotated to facilitate the reported binding of calretulin to HLA-A*02:01 (Collins et al., 1994), and the gate-open displacement of Tyr84 observed here confirms that the MHC I binding pocket is less rigid than previously realized.
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural data obtained in this study.

claim: The increased frequency of extended peptides following infection suggests that T. gondii ligands emerge from a distinct pathway of antigen processing and presentation.
source: The increased frequency of extended peptides following infection suggests that T. gondii ligands emerge from a distinct pathway of antigen processing and presentation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed data.

claim: Class I MHC peptide ligands are typically derived from the proteasomal degradation of cytosolic proteins, active transport by TAP into the lumen of the ER, further proteolytic trimming in the ER, and chaperone mediated loading into class I MHC prior to egress to the plasma membrane.
source: Class I MHC peptide ligands are typically derived from the proteasomal degradation of cytosolic proteins, active transport by TAP into the lumen of the ER, further proteolytic trimming in the ER, and chaperone mediated loading into class I MHC prior to egress to the plasma membrane.
evidence: This represents established knowledge about MHC I antigen processing.

claim: T. gondii parasites are contained within a fusion resistant parasitophorous vacuole (PV), making it necessary that alternative mechanisms contribute to T. gondii protein degradation, transport, and trimming prior to presentation.
source: In the case of T. gondii, parasites are contained within a fusion resistant parasitophorous vacuole (PV), making it necessary that alternative mechanisms contribute to T. gondii protein degradation, transport, and trimming prior to presentation.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about T. gondii biology and logical inference.

claim: Current evidence shows that T. gondii proteins secreted into the PV can be retrotransolcated via the endoplasmic reticulum associated degradation (ERAD) complex from lumen of the PV to the host cytosol where they are routed to MHC I.
source: Current evidence shows that T. gondii proteins secreted into the PV can be retrotransolcated via the endoplasmic reticulum associated degradation (ERAD) complex from lumen of the PV to the host cytosol where they are routed to MHC I (Blanchard et al., 2008; Feliu et al., 2013; Grover et al., 2014; Gubbels et al., 2005).
evidence: This is based on citations to prior research.

claim: The extended T. gondii ligands observed do not seem to fit the model of cross-presentation via ERAD as their C-terminal extensions suggest a lack of interaction with proteolytic agents of the host cytosol.
source: The extended T. gondii ligands observed here do not seem to fit this model of cross-presentation as their C-terminal extensions suggest a lack of interaction with proteolytic agents of the host cytosol and as many T. gondii ligands are derived from proteins not secreted into the PV.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed data and known biology.

claim: Evidence of a semi-permeable channel between the PV and the ER might explain the presentation of extended peptides.
source: Indeed evidence of a semi-permeable channel between the PV and the ER might explain the presentation of extended peptides (Goldszmid et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation based on a citation to prior research.

claim: THP-1 cells were acquired from ATCC (ATCC# TIB-202).
source: THP-1 cells acquired from ATCC (ATCC# TIB-202) were cultured in RPMI supplemented with 10% FBS.
evidence: This is a methodological detail.

claim: The observed HLA type of the THP-1 cells used in all experiments is HLA-A*02:01, -B*15:11, C*03:03, DRB1*01:01, DRB1*15:01.
